analysis.one_liner: Caps sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, mercury, and carbon dioxide emissions from power plants through declining tonnage limits and emissions trading.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Sen. Lamar Alexander with one cosponsor, was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee and never received a markup, vote, or floor action before the Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would set hard national limits on four pollutants from fossil-fuel power plants: sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, mercury, and carbon dioxide. The limits tighten over time, and plants would trade emission allowances to comply, with a quarter of the carbon dioxide allowances auctioned off and the proceeds used to help electricity consumers and energy-intensive industries absorb cost increases. It would also reward the first 30 new coal plants built to strict standards, crack down on old plants that have dodged modern pollution controls, and pay farmers and others for projects like manure digesters and tree planting that offset greenhouse gases.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people near power plants and downwind — including visitors to national parks, which the bill specifically targets for haze and acid rain cleanup — gain cleaner air and lower mercury exposure. Farmers, foresters, and waste operators gain a new revenue stream from offset credits. Electricity consumers get a share of auction proceeds earmarked to offset rate increases. Existing power plants also benefit, because the bill would hand most emission allowances to them free of charge rather than auctioning them all.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Downwind communities, park visitors, farmers, power consumers

how_it_helps.text: Caps sulfur dioxide emissions at 2 million tons per year beginning in 2015, down from the much larger levels the existing acid rain program allowed, with the aim of cutting the haze and acid deposition that damage national parks and class I areas.

Sets a declining national cap on power-plant carbon dioxide — 2.3 billion metric tons in 2011-2014, falling to 1.5 billion by 2025 — the first hard federal ceiling on the pollution driving climate change from the electric sector.
Requires coal plants to capture 60 percent of mercury entering the plant starting in the first compliance year and 90 percent by 2015, with a $50,000-per-pound penalty for excess emissions.

Requires plants that have operated 40 or more years to meet modern sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides performance standards starting in 2020, closing the gap for the roughly three-quarters of coal units the bill notes are more than 30 years old and operating under exemptions meant to be temporary.
Voids a December 13, 2005 EPA letter that had weakened pollution-control requirements for proposed new coal plants, restoring stricter review of new construction.

Auctions 25 percent of carbon dioxide allowances beginning in 2011 and directs the proceeds, without further appropriation, to mitigating electricity cost increases for consumers and energy-intensive industries.

Creates offset credits for farmers and landowners — for manure digesters, biomass co-firing, converting land to forest, and building energy-efficiency projects — turning emission reductions on farms into revenue.
Directs NOAA to issue regional air quality forecasts and warnings so people can plan around bad air days.

analysis.who_pays: Coal-fired and other fossil-fuel power plants bear the direct cost: they must cut sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, and mercury sharply and buy allowances or install controls for carbon dioxide. Some of those costs would flow to electricity ratepayers, though a quarter of carbon allowances would be auctioned with proceeds set aside to cushion consumer bills and energy-intensive industries. The coal mining industry faces slower growth as new plants must meet a strict carbon standard.
analysis.who_pays_short: Coal and fossil-fuel power plants, their ratepayers

drawbacks.text: Most carbon dioxide, nitrogen oxide, and sulfur dioxide allowances would be given free to existing plants based on how much fuel they historically burned rather than auctioned, which compensates the oldest, highest-emitting generators and can hand them allowance value beyond their compliance costs.

The Climate Champions Program reserves allowances for the first 30 new coal-fired plants built to the bill's standards, which could encourage new coal plant construction even as the bill limits coal pollution overall.

Compliance costs would pressure electricity rates; the bill acknowledges this by earmarking auction proceeds to mitigate cost increases for consumers and energy-intensive industries, but the cushion covers only the auctioned share.
The mercury limits are written as the less stringent of two options — percent capture or an emission rate — and allow averaging across a company's units, softening the standard for dirtier plants.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public gains are large and concrete: sharp cuts in the pollutants behind acid rain, park haze, mercury exposure, and climate change, concentrated on a sector the bill itself says produces 67 percent of sulfur dioxide and 40 percent of mercury and carbon dioxide emissions nationwide. The costs fall on utilities and, to some degree, ratepayers, but the bill blunts them with free allowance allocations to existing plants and auction proceeds earmarked for consumers. The honest criticism is design, not purpose: by giving allowances free to incumbent emitters and rewarding new coal plants, it buys industry cooperation at the price of locking fossil generation in as the regulated channel for years.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which never took it up, and it died there when the Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Sen. Lamar Alexander introduced the bill on April 19, 2007, joined by Sen. Joseph Lieberman.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works.
No further action appears in the record: no hearings, markups, committee vote, or floor action followed, and the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009, with the bill still in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal-fired utilities and other fossil generators are better off because the bill died — they kept operating under the older rules, without declining caps on sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, mercury, or carbon dioxide, and without having to buy allowances. Farmers and landowners also lost the offset revenue the bill would have created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coal-fired utilities that avoided new limits

against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no markup, no committee vote, no report — leaving it to die when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsorship was bipartisan — a Tennessee Republican joined by an Independent from Connecticut — but no committee or floor vote was ever recorded, so the partisan shape of any opposition is unknown.

industries.note: The bill would force coal plants into sharp cuts in sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, and mercury and a declining carbon cap — a real cost to the industry — but it would give most allowances free to existing units based on fuel burned and reserve rewards for the first 30 new coal plants, compensating incumbent generators and keeping coal generation entrenched as the regulated channel. For the public, the industry's compliance cost is the gain; its free allocations are a transfer.

Mercury limits, the 2-million-ton sulfur dioxide cap, and a strict carbon standard for new plants raise the cost of coal-fired generation and slow new plant construction, shrinking future coal demand — though the Climate Champions rewards partially cushion that.

industries.industry: Fossil-fuel-fired electric utilities (oil and natural gas)
industries.note: All fossil plants above 25 megawatts would face the nitrogen oxide and carbon dioxide caps and allowance costs, though allocations based on fuel use would offset much of the burden for existing units.

Offset credits for manure digesters, biomass co-firing, afforestation, and building efficiency would create a new market paying farmers and landowners for emission reductions that also improve soil, water, and habitat.
Auction proceeds would flow directly to mitigating electricity cost increases for consumers and energy-intensive industries, cushioning the rate impacts of the caps.
